meta.title: Portolan — An opinionated standard for cloud-native geospatial catalogs
meta.description: Portolan publishes geospatial data as plain files on object storage, with no servers, no databases, and no proprietary licenses. Structured metadata lets a person or an agent read a catalog and query it directly. The standard sets the quality bar, a validator enforces it, tools make catalogs cheap to build, and a registry connects them into a network anyone can search.

hero.title: The future of spatial data
hero.description: Share geospatial data as plain files in your own storage. You describe the data once, and it opens in QGIS, queries from DuckDB, loads in a notebook, and an agent can read it straight from the URL. There is no server to run and no account to make.
hero.summary: Portolan is an open standard built on <m>STAC</m> and <m>GeoParquet</m>, plus tools to build catalogs and a registry to find them.

why.title: Spatial data infrastructure still assumes servers and specialists. Portolan doesn't.

open.title: Your data works in the tools people already have.
open.description: A catalog is open formats all the way down, from <m>GeoParquet</m> to cloud-optimized GeoTIFF to <m>STAC</m>. It opens in QGIS and ArcGIS and queries from DuckDB and BigQuery. It stays useful with or without Portolan, and everything is open source under <m>Apache-2.0</m>.

aiFirst.title: You don't have to be a specialist.
aiFirst.description: A catalog explains itself. The metadata says what the data covers and what the fields mean, in text a person or an agent can read. There is no API to learn. The <link>Finland.SDI demo</link> shows an agent answering questions against a national archive this way.

easy.title: Publishing is an afternoon, not a project.
easy.description: Point the CLI at your data and push. There is no database to stand up and nothing running afterward. A catalog is files in a bucket.

scalable.title: There is nothing to scale.
scalable.description: The same setup serves megabytes or terabytes. Growth is your cloud provider's job, because storage is the only part that grows.

lowCost.title: The bill is storage plus egress.
lowCost.description: That is the whole budget, and it goes to your cloud provider, not to us. A popular dataset should not blow a budget. The <link>cost calculator</link> shows what yours would run.

sovereign.title: Your data stays in your jurisdiction.
sovereign.description: Host on AWS, GCS, Azure, MinIO, Hetzner, Scaleway, or any S3-compatible storage. No foreign vendor sits between your agency and its data.

large.title: Large publishers
large.body: Most of the people who could use a large archive never touch it, because the portal requires an account and the API requires a client library. A Portolan catalog has neither. You describe the archive once, and analysts and agents can query it without downloading it, asking questions you never planned for.

small.title: Small publishers
small.body: A city's flood maps and building footprints often go unpublished, because sharing them has meant a server and a budget line to keep it alive. A Portolan catalog is files in a bucket. Nothing runs afterward and the bill rounds to zero, and the registry makes the catalog as findable as a planetary archive.

users.title: Data users
users.body: Working with spatial data has meant building a new pipeline for every source. A Portolan catalog says what it covers and what its fields mean before you download anything, and the formats let you fetch the two hundred megabytes you need instead of the forty gigabytes around them. You can start working the afternoon you find the data, and an agent can too, because a catalog that explains itself to a person explains itself to a machine.

howItWorks.title: Three steps to publish, one to use.

convert.title: Convert
convert.description: The CLI turns what you have into cloud-native files. Shapefiles and GeoPackages become <m>GeoParquet</m>, rasters become <m>COG</m>, tiles become <m>PMTiles</m>.

catalog.title: Describe
catalog.description: The CLI writes a <m>STAC</m> catalog for your files. That is the part that lets a stranger understand your data without asking you.

publish.title: Publish
publish.description: Push the files to any S3-compatible bucket. AWS, GCS, Azure, R2, MinIO, or Source Cooperative all work.

browse.title: Use
browse.description: Open the catalog in QGIS, query it from DuckDB or Sedona, load it in a notebook, or give an agent the URL.

projects.skills: Claude skills. Publish with an agent.

cli.title: With the CLI
cli.description: Install <m>portolan-cli</m>, then <m>init</m>, <m>add</m>, <m>check</m>, and <m>push</m>. It converts your files and writes the catalog for you.

claude.title: With Claude
claude.description: Install the Portolan skill in Claude Code and point it at your data. It runs the convert, describe, and publish steps for you, so you don't have to be a data engineer.
